title: Trees Use Hidden 'Muscles' to Stand Up Straight
summary:
Trees cannot walk or stretch. Still, they can sense their own shape and change how they grow to stay upright. This sense is called proprioception. People once thought only animals had it. In 2012, researchers working with INRAE showed that plants have it too.

To study this hidden sense, scientists built a special test. Young trees spun slowly on a platform inside a ball of light that shone the same from every side. Gravity and light gave them no clues about which way to grow.

The test began with young poplar trees lying flat. As they grew, their stems curved upward. A special kind of wood, called tension wood, helped. It pulls like a muscle.

After about ten days, the curved trees went onto the spinning platform. Over the next weeks, their stems slowly became straight again. New tension wood had grown on the other side, pulling the opposite way, like a second muscle.

This could help trees stand straight again after storms bend them.
why_it_matters: Understanding trees helps children care for the trees in parks, gardens and forests that they play in and enjoy.

keywords.explanation: Proprioception is the sense that lets a living thing feel its own shape and position.
Tension wood is a special kind of wood that pulls like a muscle to help a tree change how it grows.
Gravity is the force that pulls things down toward the Earth.
A poplar is a kind of fast-growing tree, and young poplars were used in the test.
A stem is the main stalk of a plant or young tree that holds it up.

Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists and researchers working with INRAE, studying young poplar trees.
WHAT: They studied how trees sense their own shape and straighten themselves using tension wood.
WHERE: In a special test, with trees spun slowly on a platform inside a ball of light that shone the same from every side.
WHY: Gravity and light gave the trees no clues about which way to grow, so scientists could study the trees' hidden sense on its own.
